Description:
Cyberattacks can come from many different vectors, but they most commonly arrive via email. By using email to conduct phishing, business email compromise (BEC) attacks, brand impersonation and more, attackers leverage an organization’s weakest security link — its people — to wreak havoc. As a result, email is the No. 1 attack vector for security teams to secure. By integrating Mimecast with Splunk, security teams can leverage advanced threat detection, enhanced investigation, and faster response to increase their overall level of protection through proactive actions that identify at-risk users and devices. Together, the platforms share high-fidelity indicators to help analysts quickly and accurately identify the root cause of an attack and remediate the threat. This helps security teams ward against initial infection and lateral spread that can lead to downtime, ransom demands, lost data, and stolen passwords. Splunk can ingest Mimecast logs, along with other security tools, to obtain complete visibility across environments. Out-of-the-box detection templates created by Mimecast’s team of security experts based on known threats, common attack vectors and suspicious activity reduce detection times to make analysts aware of a threat the moment it occurs. Mimecast regional threat intelligence data can power analytics to generate actionable alerts and incidents, allowing security teams to easily investigate and triage incidents based on the severity and status of detected threats. Additionally, Mimecast provides a Splunk SOAR application as well as a comprehensive Application Programming Interface (API) to make it easy for the platform to be integrated with Splunk’s leading security orchestration, automation, and response (SOAR) for efficient, automated response actions. Description:
Inno AI Chat lets your team ask questions about Splunk data in plain language and get an answer together with the SPL that produced it, so every answer can be read, re-run and checked. It is built for environments that cannot send operational data to a hosted AI service. The language model runs on hardware you control (any OpenAI-compatible endpoint, for example vLLM), the app runs inside your Splunk with your users' roles and permissions, and no telemetry, query or answer is ever sent to the vendor. Answers are grounded in your own environment. The app measures which indexes, sourcetypes, fields and values actually exist in your Splunk, and works from that instead of from what a model assumes Splunk data looks like. Curated knowledge is available for three domains: network, security and IT operations. Generated SPL and interpretations can be wrong or incomplete. Inno AI Chat shows its work so you can see why, and it is meant to support operational and security decisions, not to replace them. This is a paid product licensed per Splunk search head cluster and per domain. There is no free tier or trial: the download and the license key are delivered with your purchase. See https://innosw.net/ai-chat/ for licensing and purchase.

Trigger Kestra flows from Splunk alerts. Send alert metadata, mapped result fields and the full search results to any Kestra workflow to automate remediation, ticketing and response.


Description:
The Kestra Add-on for Splunk turns Splunk alerts into automated workflows. It adds a "Trigger Kestra Flow" alert action that starts an execution of any Kestra flow whenever a Splunk alert fires, so detections lead directly to remediation, ticketing, notifications, data pipelines or any other process orchestrated in Kestra. Problem it solves: Splunk is good at detecting that something happened, but responding usually means custom scripts, webhooks with no authentication, or manual hand-offs. This add-on connects Splunk to Kestra natively and securely: the alert's metadata, selected result fields, and the full search results file are sent to the flow as typed inputs through the Kestra Executions API. Key features: - "Trigger Kestra Flow" alert action, configured per alert (tenant, namespace, flow ID) - Reusable Kestra connections; API tokens are stored encrypted in Splunk's credential store - Full search results attached as a CSV file input - Alert metadata forwarded as flow inputs (search name, SID, app, owner, trigger time, results link) - Flexible input mapping from Splunk tokens such as $result.field$ and $name$ to flow inputs - Role for non-admin alert owners (kestra_alert_user)

Short Description:

Description:
TA-Nvidia is a free, source-available Splunk add-on that brings enterprise NVIDIA GPU observability to any Splunk instance running on hosts with NVIDIA drivers. It repeatedly captures the COMPLETE nvidia-smi state; temperature, utilization, fan speed, power draw and limits, framebuffer memory, graphics/SM/clocks, ECC errors, PCIe throughput, performance state, compute processes, vGPU, and more and indexes it two ways with zero manual configuration: 1. Full JSON events (sourcetype nvidia:smi) in index=main for deep-dive fielded search, and 2. Time-series metrics (nvidia.* metric names) in index=metrics via a metric-schema pipeline, enabling fast mstats trends and visualizations. Two pre-built dashboards ship with the app GPU Overview (per-GPU cards for temp, utilization, memory, power, clock, fan) and GPU Metrics (long-window trended charts via mstats). Why this matters: GPU-equipped servers are expensive and failure-prone. Overheating, ECC errors, clock throttling, memory exhaustion, and power-limiting silently destroy GPU workload performance (AI/ML training and inference, VDI, HPC, video/transcode). Splunk has no free, turnkey NVIDIA telemetry app, TA-Nvidia closes that gap in about one minute, on any distribution (Tested on datacenter and workstation cards, current driver: 580.x, RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell). Licensing: free for personal, evaluation, and non-commercial use. Commercial/production use requires a license from the author: michael@bentleypc.com. item.title: TA-IPMI - v1.0.0 [New App Release]
item.description:
Platform: Splunk


Release Notes:
Initial release of TA-IPMI. New: - Collects all IPMI SDR sensors via ipmitool (local open interface): temperatures, fan RPM, voltages, power draw, thresholds and sensor status (ok/nc/cr/nr) as JSON events in index=main, sourcetype ipmi:status, including chassis power state, last power event, intrusion and BMC firmware fields. - Numeric sensors indexed as time-series metrics to index=metrics (sourcetype ipmi:metrics) with clean ipmi.* metric names (for example ipmi.cpu_temp, ipmi.45fan1, ipmi.p1_12v, ipmi.input_power). - System Event Log (SEL) captured with per-record dedup (high-water mark): each SEL record appears exactly once as an event with sensor, event type, assertion state and raw text, sourcetype ipmi:sel. - IPMI Overview dashboard: chassis/BMC status, current sensor readings table, newest-first SEL log. - IPMI Metrics dashboard: trended charts for temperatures, fans, voltages and power draw plus a live distinct-metric counter. - Auto-detects hosts without a BMC: inputs log a notice and exit cleanly instead of erroring. - Passed Splunk AppInspect cloud validation pre-certification (0 failures, 0 errors). Requirements: ipmitool installed (apt-get install -y ipmitool / yum install -y ipmitool), a reachable local BMC (/dev/ipmi0 via ipmi_si + ipmi_devintf), Splunk 9.x, and a metrics index (datatype=metric). Known limitations: - Voltage/Power chart families are matched by common IPMI sensor name patterns (12V, Vcore, watts, PSU, input, output...). IPMI sensor naming is vendor-defined; add unusual vendor spellings to the panel's search IN (...) list. - SEL is deduplicated permanently by default; to re-index current SEL contents once, delete $SPLUNK_HOME/var/lib/splunk/TA-IPMI/sel_last_id. - Commercial/production use requires a license from the author (michael@bentleypc.com); free for personal, evaluation and non-commercial use.


Short Description:
Free server BMC monitoring for Splunk. Streams IPMI sensors (temps, fan RPM, volts, watts), chassis/PSU status, and the System Event Log from ipmitool's local interface into events and metrics, with Overview and Metrics dashboards. Passes AppInspect cloud pre-cert. Commercial use requires license.


Description:
TA-IPMI is a free, source-available Splunk add-on that brings out-of-band hardware health monitoring to any Splunk host with a server-class BMC. It reads full IPMI telemetry via ipmitool's local open interface and indexes it three ways with zero manual configuration: 1. Sensor readings: every SDR sensor (temperatures, fan RPM, voltages such as 12V/3.3V/Vcore/BAT, power draw in watts, plus thresholds), plus chassis and BMC status as rich JSON events (index=main, sourcetype ipmi:status) for fielded search. 2. The same readings as time-series metrics in index=metrics (sourcetype ipmi:metrics, ipmi.* measure names), so thermal, fan, voltage and power trends survive retention and answer in milliseconds with mstats. 3. The System Event Log (SEL): each SEL record indexed exactly once as a separate event with sensor, event type, assertion state and raw detail preserved, so BIOS-level crashes, power faults, ECC errors, fan failures and intrusion alerts become searchable Splunk events. Why it matters: IPMI/BMC is the only observability layer that survives OS crashes, power loss, and hangs. Overheating servers, dead fans, failing PSUs, dropped redundancy and unexpected reboots happen below the OS where agents and syslog can't follow, but the BMC remembers everything. TA-IPMI closes that blind spot in minutes: install it on the host, and its BMC telemetry flows into Splunk with ready-made overview and trend dashboards. Licensing: free for personal, evaluation, and non-commercial use. Commercial/production use requires a license from the author: michael@bentleypc.com. Source available at https://github.com/bentleymi/TA-IPMI

item.description:

Release Notes:
Credential Hunter 1.0.0 — first public release Credential Hunter searches the raw data of the indexes you already have for secrets that were indexed by accident: cleartext passwords, API keys, tokens, private keys and password hashes. It is not a data source and it ingests nothing — it works on what is already in Splunk.


Short Description:
Scans Splunk indexes for accidentally indexed credentials using two-stage term-index prefiltering and regex verification, with configurable pattern catalogs and continuous monitoring.


Description:
The Credential Hunter app scans raw data in existing Splunk indexes to identify credentials that were indexed by accident, including cleartext passwords, API keys, tokens, and private keys. It employs a two-stage detection approach that combines term-index prefiltering in Splunk with regex verification in Python to minimize performance impact while maintaining accuracy. The app supports both full historical scans and continuous monitoring modes, with a configurable pattern catalog that allows administrators to enable or disable specific credential types based on their environment. Findings are stored in KV store collections and presented through dedicated dashboards for investigation, false positive management, and pattern tuning. The scanner operates as a scripted input that runs continuously but performs actual scans at administrator-defined intervals of 30 or 60 minutes. Configuration is managed through a Control room dashboard where scan intervals, event slack hours for late-arriving data, and retention policies can be adjusted without editing configuration files.

item.title: Nikhil Chawla Add-on for Absolute Secure Endpoint - v1.0.1 [New App Release]
item.description:

Release Notes:
\- A run that Splunk stops (input disabled, edited or restarted, Run now, or Splunk stopping) now ends cleanly with "run stopped" instead of failing with BrokenPipeError, and keeps its checkpoint. If Splunk had already closed the pipe, the window that was cut short is sent again, so no events are lost. \- An event is marked as sent only once it has been written. \- Run now is refused while a run of that input is in progress.


Short Description:
Collects Absolute Secure Endpoint SIEM events (device, console and alert activity) and device inventory from the Absolute API, with CIM mappings (Authentication, Change, Alerts, Data Access, Inventory) and an ES asset lookup. Accounts, inputs and status are managed in Splunk Web. Independent project, not affiliated with Absolute Software.


Description:
Collects Absolute Secure Endpoint data from the Absolute API and maps it to the Splunk Common Information Model. - SIEM events (sourcetype absolute:events): what devices report (applications installed, removed and updated; hardware, network, OS and user changes; location and geofence changes; encryption, antivirus and application-persistence status), what console users do (sign-ins, account and role changes, rules, geofences, policy groups, device freeze, disable and unenroll, location lookups), and alerts (alert rules that fired, connections blocked in restricted regions). The same events Absolute's SIEM Connector sends to a syslog server, read straight from the API, with each event's id and as JSON. - Devices (sourcetype absolute:devices): an inventory snapshot, one event per device: hardware, OS, users, agent, addresses, encryption, antivirus, location. CIM: Authentication, Change (Account_Management, Endpoint_Changes), Alerts, Data Access and Inventory. A saved search builds an Enterprise Security asset lookup from the device inventory. - Inputs page in Splunk Web: Absolute accounts (API host, token ID and secret key, optional proxy; stored encrypted in Splunk's credential store; a Test button checks the token) and inputs: add, edit, enable, disable, run now, delete. - SIEM events are collected from a checkpoint in overlapping windows and de-duplicated by event id: restarts and failures do not lose events. If Splunk stops a run part-way (input disabled or restarted), the next run continues from the checkpoint; at most the window it was cut off in is sent again. - Status dashboard: last run, events and devices collected, minutes behind, errors, how late events arrive. Overview dashboard: event types, console activity, alerts, posture changes, devices by OS, agent, encryption and antivirus. - Python standard library only, no third-party packages. Independent project, not affiliated with or endorsed by Absolute Software. Absolute and Absolute Secure Endpoint are trademarks of Absolute Software Corporation.

item.title: BXTI Add-on for Proofpoint SER - v1.0.2 [New App Release]
item.description:
Platform: Splunk


Release Notes:
## Version 1.0.2 ### Features * Native, read-only Proofpoint Secure Email Relay reporting with eight selectable overview and summary report types. * Encrypted credential storage, configurable destination index and polling interval, and prefilled, editable sourcetypes. * Initial daily backfill options of No backfill, 7, 14 or 30 days, with checkpointed catch-up and suppression of unchanged rows. * Optional domain and recipient delivery-failure breakdowns for relay-user and tag failure inputs, disabled by default. ###


Short Description:
Collect Proofpoint Secure Email Relay usage and delivery-failure reports natively in Splunk, with encrypted credential storage, configurable polling, checkpointed daily backfill and optional domain/recipient failure details.


Description:
BXTI Add-on for Proofpoint SER brings Proofpoint Secure Email Relay (SER) usage and delivery-failure reporting into Splunk through native, read-only API collection. It helps administrators monitor reported message volumes, throughput and delivery failures without a separate automation platform. Choose from eight overview and summary report types, including message usage, throughput, relay-user and tag reports, and message-failure summaries. Configure API credentials, destination index, polling interval, initial backfill and sourcetype directly in the add-on. Optional domain and recipient failure breakdowns are disabled by default and can be enabled for relay-user or tag failure inputs. Daily collection supports checkpointed catch-up and suppression of unchanged report rows. This add-on collects reporting aggregates, not individual email messages or message content. It is specific to Proofpoint SER, not Proofpoint TAP, Essentials or other Proofpoint APIs. It does not include dashboards or alert rules and does not claim CIM data-model compliance.

item.description:
Platform: Splunk


Release Notes:
# Adjutant AI (formerly AI Workbench) — Release notes What's new, improved, and fixed in each release, in plain language. This is the **customer-facing** summary used for the Splunkbase release-notes section; the full technical changelog lives in the project's detailed release notes. **Last updated:** 2026-10-23 > **About version numbers.** Releases once numbered 0.10–0.13 were renumbered to > 1.0–1.3 to reflect production maturity — no behaviour changed. The current release is > **2.7.2**, a maintenance release on **2.7.0** after **2.7.1**: Adjutant AI runs **governed agents**, a **Tool calls** panel shows each step of a > request and lets you stop it, and **multi-source reconciliation** arrives as a Preview. > 2.7.0 sits on top of **2.5.9**'s setup wizard that says which model actually answered and why a > gateway lists none, a ninth option for self-hosted and in-house models, and connection checks that > no longer award a pass they did not earn; 2.5.9 on top of **2.5.8**'s playbooks that carry all of their instructions, and every path to > an AI service agreeing about where a request goes, and 2.5.8 on top of **2.5.4**'s readable RCA report and **2.5.3**'s private LLM endpoints and **2.5.2**'s one connection for several tenants and **2.5.1**'s fixes to **2.5.0**'s setup wizard and **2.4.2** — a data-correctness fix on top of **2.4.1**, a connectivity release on top of the **2.4.0** integration workstream and **2.2.2**, itself a maintenance release on **2.2.1**, itself a maintenance release on > **2.2.0**'s **Explain a SPL search**, and **2.1.0**'s **Fraud capability** and the **2.0 line** (the deterministic **ITSI Root > Cause Analysis** engine, **resource-consumption monitoring**, and **2.0.7**'s durable memory, > Scheduled Ask and governed integrations), which in turn built on > **1.8.5** (the **CIM Coverage Audit**), **1.8.4** (async playbook execution over MCP > plus the **Outcome Ledger** executive/audit dashboard), **1.8.3** > (a security‑hardening release: OWASP + dependency + anti‑ransomware audit), **1.8.2** (Splunk > Edge Processor data‑quality awareness and keyless Azure OpenAI authentication), **1.8.1** > (support‑diagnosis fixes) and **1.8.0** (agent telemetry & OCSF export, content packs, > all‑tiers data‑quality checks, Splunk 10.x readiness, Dashboard Studio version‑awareness). The > **1.7.0** ServiceNow integration and the **1.5.0 "Data Foundation & MCP OAuth"** themes are > included below. --- ## 2.8.0 (in development) ### Questions you answer with a click - When the assistant needs a decision, it shows a question card in the reply area instead of ending its answer with a question: up to four questions, choices as buttons with the recommended one first, an **Other…** field on every question, and one click when there is a single choice to make. Text typed in the reply box while a card is open is sent as your answer (**Send as answer**). - **Stop** while a card is open ends the request; the card shows **Not answered**. The TOOL CALLS panel shows the question as a **Your answer** step, and the time strip counts the wait as *Waiting for user*. - The shipped agent templates, skills and knowledge now ask through the card. An agent running unattended never waits for an answer: it takes the recommended option and says which, and it never makes a change on that basis. ### Upgrade note: Fraud Rule Builder and Fraud Command Center run in the Console only - Both need values only a person can give: the detection threshold, the customer's thresholds and AML jurisdiction lists. They ask for them in the Console every time, and their Agent modes switches are disabled. - **Fraud Rule Builder no longer runs from alerts.** Its Triggered mode is gone. Any mode an install had switched on for either agent is switched off on upgrade, with an `agent_mode_upgrade_conflict` line in the platform audit log. An unattended start is refused before the language model is called. ### Agents know which indexes you can search, and what is in them - When an agent lists indexes, the list is the one **you** can search: it comes from a search run as you, so it never names an index your roles cannot read. Metric and empty indexes are included. - On a large estate an agent finds any index by a name pattern (for example `fw_*`). A list longer than 200 indexes says it was cut short, gives the total, and the agent narrows it with a pattern. - A daily **index catalogue** tells the agent, for each index you can search, its main sourcetypes, its events per day and its last event. The agent reads it with the first list in a request, so it runs fewer searches just to find where your data is. It is built once a day (the time is an admin setting) and is available on every edition. - If one of your roles filters which events you see, the catalogue shows you only index names, types and last-event dates, not sourcetypes or volumes. - Tested on a single search head. Distributed deployments (a search head with separate indexers) are proven by tests only, not yet live. ### Fewer repeated searches across requests - Your own identical search from an earlier request is reused while Splunk still holds its results (10 minutes after it was last used), after checking it is still there. Nobody else's search is ever reused for you. - Word counts and the hours in which a word occurs are kept for 15 minutes and shared within your organisation, but only for indexes you can search, and never with or from a user whose roles filter events. - Time estimates and search budgets use the speed measured on each index, so the first estimate of a request is realistic instead of a fixed default. ### Integration runs show their steps - The step view of an integration run now shows what the run did at each step: what was read, what each filter dropped, what the mapping produced and what was written. A run that lands several resources or sources shows each of them separately. The run's history keeps the counts per step. ### Preview before write holds scheduled integration runs too - A scheduled integration with preview before write switched on now stops before it writes and shows its preview on the run, instead of stopping with nothing to approve. Approve the preview, then choose **Send approved payload**: a new run writes exactly the records you approved. - Sending an approved write sends exactly what was approved, even if new records arrived in the meantime; they follow in the next run. An approval is used once, and expires after an hour: an expired one is not sent, and the run shows a fresh preview instead. - When an integration names an approver role, anyone with that role in the integration's own organisation can see, approve and send its previews. Without a named role, only the person who started the run or an administrator can, as before. - Switching off the approval requirement for scheduled runs still lets them write without a preview. A scheduled reconciliation still needs that setting: it stops without a preview when approval is required. ### Reconciliation actions on the integration page - Administrators can now act on a reconciliation integration from its page: **Reconcile now**, **Test write access** per ServiceNow table, **Check relationship types**, **Change a record's key…**, **Request promotion**, **Export**, and **Preview** with **Push all records, not only changes**. - Promotions and key changes need two administrators: the requester sees **Waiting for a second administrator**, another administrator sees **Approve**, and either applies it once approved. - Going live, applying a promotion or key change, and deciding a held run each ask for confirmation first, stating the preview's own numbers and id. A push-all preview can now go live; before, it was refused as out of date. - A promotion or key-change request can be taken back with **Withdraw request** until it is applied, by the administrator who requested it or any other. A withdrawn request cannot be applied. Before, an approved request stayed open until it expired an hour later. - **Test write access** takes optional **Probe fields** for a table whose records need mandatory fields. Each field is checked against the table before the probe is written. - The page shows each test's and check's last recorded result when it opens: when, by whom, and whether it passed. - When an Organisation has no audit index, the pages say these actions are not recorded, and so does each action's result. Before, they ran unrecorded without a word. ### Build and run integrations as flows - **Unattended runs → Flows** brings back the Integration Editor, and a flow you draw there now runs. Set each node's settings in the editor, save, and activate: a scheduled flow then runs on its schedule, and **Run now** runs it straight away. - **Run draft** is a dry run of the version you are editing: it reads and maps, shows its steps, and writes nothing. - The canvas shows how the last run went on every node. - A flow with an MCP trigger can be started by another AI agent over MCP, with the new `adjutantai_list_flows` and `adjutantai_start_flow` tools. Only administrators can use them. - A flow write held for approval can be approved and sent like an integration's: one preview for the whole run, then **Send approved payload** writes exactly what you approved to every destination. A send is refused when another version of the flow was activated in the meantime. - Activating, deactivating and running a flow are recorded in your organisation's audit log first; when that is enforced and the event cannot be written, nothing changes. - In this version a flow reads from ServiceNow, a Splunk lookup or a Splunk index, and writes through a mapping, or runs a reconciliation contract. Lookups and indexes are read as the business unit's service account when there is one, and only indexes that account can search are read. ### Security fixes - A support bundle now holds only the request you report, not other requests from the same browser tab. - A support bundle no longer carries text a tool returned in two more places: the search advisor's and the training check's notes, and the validation messages of objects the assistant saved. They are now recorded as decisions and counts. - When the optional diagnostic capture is switched on, its one-hour limit is now enforced: an expired capture is deleted and never handed out. - Reconciliation actions are now recorded in the audit log: reconcile, export, the write-access and relationship-type checks, previews and live runs, promotions, key changes and held-run decisions. Each is recorded before it changes anything; when the Org enforces audit logging and the record cannot be written, the action is refused and nothing changes. - When an Org's audit settings cannot be read, Adjutant now treats the Org as enforcing audit logging, everywhere: a Console question, an unattended run, a reconciliation or workspace action is refused with "The audit settings could not be read, so this was not run. Nothing was changed. Try again in a moment." Before, it fell back to running unaudited. The one exception is the support bundle: it can still be downloaded, so a broken installation can be diagnosed. Its audit record is still attempted, and Adjutant logs a warning when it cannot be written. ### Changed - Starting an agent over MCP while the same agent is already queued or running in the same organisation and business unit now returns the run that is already going, instead of starting a second one. When the instance runs in stateless mode, an agent started over MCP also waits until the instance is ready, like scheduled runs. ### Smaller fixes - The audit check no longer reports a false 'audit event not found' error for entries that were written correctly but indexed late. - A scheduled integration created with an older version could not write anything: its permitted actions were empty, and each run ended without saying why. Integrations now take their permitted actions from their contract every time they run, and a run that is not allowed to write says so on the run and in a system message. - A reconciliation that had not published for more than 7 days could never publish again. It can now resume: for every table it writes, pass a new write-access check, then make a new preview after those checks and publish it. The resume is recorded in the audit log. A run refused by these checks now says, per table, why. ## 2.7.2 **In short.** A maintenance release for connections to an AI service behind a corporate proxy, and for configurations created before the setup wizard existed. - **Saving a connection from the setup wizard keeps your proxy settings.** Saving an existing connection could remove its proxy bypass list and proxy sign-in. If you saved an existing connection from the wizard with 2.7.0 or 2.7.1, check its proxy settings. - **Re-checking an existing connection uses the key you stored.** You no longer have to type the key again to run the checks, and the key never leaves the server. - **The connection status shows what is true now.** A failed check no longer stays on the status for ever: it counts for as long as a passed check does, eight hours for the quick check and seven days for the full one. The status shows this search head's own result. - **The checks behind a corporate proxy go the way your requests do.** The background check and the wizard's checks use the connection's proxy, bypass list and certificate authority. A gateway whose name only the proxy can look up is no longer reported as a refused destination. - **When a saved connection does not match what was tested, the message names the fields.** --- ## 2.7.1 **In short.** A maintenance release on 2.7.0 that fixes dashboard publishing on Splunk 10.2. - **Dashboards can be published again on Splunk 10.2.** Before publishing, Adjutant opens the new dashboard in a browser to check that it works. On Splunk 10.2 that check mistook Splunk's own navigation bar for an error on the dashboard and refused every dashboard, even one whose panels all worked. It now looks only at the dashboard itself, and still catches a real error. - **A clearer message when a dashboard is not published.** When every panel works but the dashboard itself shows an error, the message now leads with that error, instead of saying that "0 of 4 panels did not render". - **The support bundle no longer misreads runs on OpenAI-compatible models.** A long request that finished normally on Azure OpenAI or another OpenAI-compatible model was diagnosed as "ran out of tool turns". It is now treated as finished. --- ## 2.7.0 **In short.** Adjutant AI now calls what it runs by its name: governed agents. You can watch each step of a request while it runs, and stop it. Searches and dashboards are checked harder before you see them, large searches finish sooner and say when they sampled, every user is held to their own Organisation, and several sources can be reconciled into one reviewed view. ### Playbooks are now agents Adjutant AI calls its unit of work by its name: governed agents for Splunk, with every action gated and logged. The **Playbooks** tab is now **Agents**, and a new agent starts from **New agent from template**. Shipped playbooks are agent templates: ready ones, plus agent templates in preview for administrators. The settings for agents that run on their own, which earlier releases called the Backend Ask Service, are now **Unattended runs**. Nothing you configured changes. Configuration keys, REST paths and KV Store collections keep their names. A Splunk SOAR playbook is still a Splunk SOAR playbook. The tabs are now named after how an agent runs. **Ask** is now **Console**: a person runs an agent there, watches its tool calls and approves its actions. Its send button is **Run**, and the text box is **Your request**. **Scheduled Ask** is now **Unattended**, with the page heading **Unattended runs**, and its **Jobs** section is now **Agent jobs**, so it is not mistaken for Splunk's search jobs. For two releases, both tabs say what they used to be called. An agent template becomes an agent when you switch on one or more of its **agent modes**, on the new **Agent modes** tab of its Edit dialog: **Triggered** (by an alert, an Enterprise Security notable or an ITSI episode), **Scheduled**, **Integration** and **Published to MCP**. People can always pick an agent template in the Console; that needs no mode. Agent templates that were already set up for these uses keep working, with their modes shown as on. The **Agents** list can be filtered by agent mode, and administrators see **Agent templates in preview** and **Your drafts** as separate groups. The four MCP tools are renamed: `adjutantai_list_agents`, `adjutantai_start_agent`, `adjutantai_get_agent_status` and `adjutantai_get_agent_results` replace the `…_playbook…` names. If you connected an MCP client to them, update its configuration after the upgrade. ### See each step of a request, and stop it A new **Tool calls** panel shows each step of a request while it runs: what the agent called and what came back. **Stop** ends the whole request. **Cancel search** stops one long search and lets the rest go on. When a search has run for two minutes, **Keep waiting** lets you decide whether it may continue. A stopped request is recorded as cancelled, not as answered. - **A headline and a time strip.** One sentence says where things stand ("Now: …", "Took 43 s, 9 steps."), and one bar shows where the time went: Splunk, the model, network and proxy, waiting for you, and time not accounted for. - **Attention marks.** A step is marked only when something is worth a look: failed, timed out, refused, blocked by policy, a partial result, slow, a change that could not be confirmed, or a retried model call. - **Step details.** Each step opens into tabs: **Summary**, **Input** (the search and its arguments), **Output** (the result, and what the model actually read when it was cut to fit) and **Timing**. Administrators, and roles granted the trace-view capability, also see **Splunk job**, with **Open in Search** and **Job Inspector**, and **IDs**. - **Skills given and knowledge used.** Two more tabs list the instructions placed in the agent's prompt, in order and why each was there, and every knowledge entry it looked up, with a link to the step that read it. - **One panel per request.** When you answer a question the agent asked, your answer and what follows stay in the same panel, as a new turn, and the headline covers the whole request. - **The panel explains itself.** **?** opens an explanation beside the panel: what happened, in plain sentences written by fixed rules, and what each part of the panel means. **Explain these steps** asks the AI to explain the steps from their records only, labelled as the AI's reading. - A search you cancelled and the agent tries again reads **Not run: you cancelled this exact search earlier in this request** instead of looking like a normal step. - While the audit entry for a request is being written, the headline says **Now: Recording the audit entry…**, so a slow audit check before the first step no longer looks like a stalled request. - **Report issue** includes every step's facts (timings, counts, the search and its arguments) and never a tool's output or search results. ### Edit dialogs that keep your work - **Agents.** Each list in the edit dialog shows what is selected first, and you add more from a searchable list. The tools section says how many tools the agent may use. The **Visibility** tab opens with one sentence saying who can see the agent, and you choose it there: everyone, one Organisation, one Business Unit, or only its owner. - **LLM configurations.** The edit dialog no longer loses your edits: a click beside it does nothing, and you leave through **Cancel** or **Save**. Fields are grouped under headings, tabs say "changed" or "has errors" in words, and **Save** tells you what still needs fixing. Clicking the "Who may use this connection?" text no longer risks removing the first Organisation from the list. - **Dialogs and lists now look and behave the same everywhere.** Edit dialogs close only through **Cancel** or **Save**, and **Save** says what still needs fixing; read-only views close through **×** or **Close**; lists share one search, one set of buttons and one way to say they are empty; and a delete asks in the page, not in a browser pop-up. This covers **Tools** (**Manage tool**, on every tab), **Skills**, **Knowledge** (connectors, static rules and curated entries), **Models**, **Backups**, **Organisations and Business Units**, **Unattended**, the agent template view and the integration screens. Section titles read clearly in every theme. - **Values you choose from a set are picked, not typed with commas.** Tags, categories, the apps and tools a skill depends on, MITRE techniques, a ServiceNow connection's CMDB write allowlist, the fields of an integration mapping and the names that approve a reconciliation decision are lists you add to. In a mapping, where order matters, you move a value with ↑ and ↓. A list does not take the same value twice; a value that a list already held twice before the upgrade is kept, and removing one copy leaves the other. - **Models.** Prices are in US dollars per 1 million input or output tokens, with a worked example as you type. A price override needs both prices, and no price can be negative. An override saved earlier without prices shows as **0 / 0 (free)**, with how to fix it. - **Backups.** The secrets a backup refers to are counted once per secret, not once per tool that uses it, and shown as a note for restoring elsewhere rather than as an error. The backup details are readable again and show every collection's rows, grouped by area; they close only through **×** or **Close**. ### Every user stays inside their own Organisation - A user who belongs to no Organisation is refused on every endpoint, with the message your administrator configured. Users assigned to an Organisation through another app are recognised everywhere. - The lists of agents and skills come from the server, filtered to what you may see: your Organisation, your Business Unit and your own private agents. Administrators see all of them. Only administrators can read the agent and skill collections directly. - Agents and skills are always saved into your own Organisation. Only an administrator can save into another one, and that is audited. - Roles are always read from Splunk, never taken from the request. - The **Adjutant AI: Run investigation agent** alert action, owned by a user with no Organisation, is refused instead of running under the default Organisation. - The operator dashboards (Outcomes, Knobs, Resource monitor, Activity, LLM health, RCA investigation) are visible to administrators only, and other users see agent ids instead of names in the resource monitor. - With audit enforcement on, a Domain Workspace action that cannot be audited is refused, or reported as not confirmed. ### Security fixes - Editing an agent no longer resets who can see it. A private agent stays private, and the choice on the Visibility tab is kept. - Editing a skill no longer resets its sharing and ownership. - A custom tool's connection details (its address and the values of its headers) are no longer sent to users who are not administrators. Users still see the tool's name, description and inputs. Stored secrets were never sent. - Edits an administrator makes to a Domain Workspace model (panels, knowledge, tabs and perspectives) stay within the Organisation they were made for. Until now one Organisation's edit was shown to every Organisation using the same model, and could replace another Organisation's edit. ### Smaller fixes - Editing a knowledge entry or a static rule keeps what the editor does not show, such as the content pack version and the scan flags written after you opened it, instead of overwriting them. - Opening the custom tools list no longer rewrites the shipped Observability tool definitions every time. They are written only when one is missing or has changed. - **Quieter logs.** By default the app writes only warnings, errors and essential events, and more detail per component when you raise its level. The audit log no longer warns about entries that were written: an entry that needed a second attempt, or that Splunk was still indexing, is logged once, at its outcome. - **Stop** before the first step now shows how long the request really ran, instead of "0 ms". - The base guardrails now apply to every run, in the Console, unattended, over MCP and on a schedule, as their agent template always said. - Splunk's MCP Server now lists exactly the four agent tools: the retired `…_playbook…` tools are removed, and the app no longer reloads the MCP Server's tool list every five minutes. - A custom tool whose per-user credential is missing tells the user to ask an administrator, instead of pointing to a settings page that does not exist. - A ServiceNow connection over MCP reports a failed start-up when it happens, instead of failing later with an unclear error. - Every KV Store lookup the app ships carries an explicit permission. - Support bundles no longer report a false "model fallback used" warning on every call through the proxy. - The two ITSI root-cause agent templates, **ITSI — Automatic Root Cause Analysis** and **ITSI — Root-cause an episode**, are now ready for use instead of in preview (Enterprise edition, with ITSI installed). - The **User & admin documentation** link on the Help page now opens the documentation site. - The app package no longer contains test data. - A Scheduled Integration that is stopped because the licence no longer includes integrations now appears in the run history and the audit trail, with the reason. ### Dashboards and AI Toolkit results that say only what is true - Dashboards render for non-admin users on Splunk 10.4: each panel runs from a saved base search. A failed publish removes the base searches it created, and a dashboard that is not published also removes its temporary copy. - A dashboard whose searches did not validate is not rendered or published, and the answer says why. - Help text is checked against the panels: colour claims must match the colour bands, values the chart does not contain stop the publish, and "all data passed ingestion checks" cannot be claimed when the check found failures or covered only part of the index. - A panel title that names a fixed time range on a dashboard with a time picker is refused, with a neutral title suggested. A title that states a bucket size ("1h buckets") is not mistaken for one. - AI Toolkit proof dashboards read a snapshot of the scored results, so opening one never runs the model again. Anyone who can open the dashboard can see the scores. - Outlier help text cannot call an outlier region normal or quote ranges the model did not learn, and an outlier alert fires only when there is an outlier. The alert advice in the outlier agents scores only the last complete hour, once an hour. - Searches that train or score a model on hourly or daily buckets read whole buckets only, so a partial first or last hour is never flagged as an outlier. The answer says when the window was adjusted. - When the AI Toolkit cannot save a model, Adjutant AI says so with Splunk's reason and stops. It no longer builds scoring searches or dashboards on a model that does not exist. - Training or scoring a model directly on millions of raw events is refused, with the aggregate-first search to use instead. ### Searches that are checked before they are trusted - A generating command typed without its leading pipe (`tstats ...`), or placed after a pipe (`index=x | tstats ...`), is refused with the correct `| tstats ...` form. - When Adjutant AI stores a different search than the one the model wrote, for example a faster `tstats` form, the answer shows the stored search. - Saving a search applies the same checks as running it. A saved search whose result lacks a column its final `table` names is reported, not stored silently. - A check reports its true row count ("the first page shows 20 of 45 rows"), a check that runs out of time no longer reports its partial count as a result, and replies are checked against the time range the search was saved with and the window the check actually covered. - Opening a saved search that uses `apply` no longer stalls on Splunk's "Run Query Anyway" prompt. - A `tstats` search that filters on a search-time field (such as `log_level=ERROR`) always returns nothing, so it is refused when it runs and when it is saved, with the two searches that work: `TERM(ERROR)` in `tstats`, or an event search. - A saved search whose description claims a filter its search does not have ("counts errors" without an error filter) is refused, with what to add. Nothing is saved. - A link in an answer that no tool returned is named under the answer: "Adjutant could not confirm this link". The answer itself is never edited. - Large searches answer from a sample when that gives the same answer and say so, checks run over a short window first, and the proof dashboard is built only when you ask for one (see the *Changed* sections below). ### Upgrade notes - **Lookups over run data no longer ship.** The app no longer ships lookups over run history, feedback, queues, receipts or other Organisation data. The operator dashboards and alerts read that data through an administrator-only endpoint. If you searched these lookups by hand, use `| rest splunk_server=local /services/itmip_llm/admin_lookup collection=` instead. - **Customised operator dashboards need updating.** If you changed Outcomes, Knobs, Resource monitor, Activity, LLM health, RCA investigation or the Outcome ledger, your local copy must read its data through the same endpoint. - **Integrations need an Enterprise licence** (see below). - **No hidden default LLM connection.** A run that names no LLM connection used to fall back on a built-in Anthropic connection that no install creates. It now ends before any model call, with "No LLM connection for this run: set the alert action's llm_config_id, or [agent_runner] default_llm_config_id in itmip_ai_workbench.conf." An install that still has only the single API key of the earliest versions gets a real connection once, on the first start after the upgrade: the key is copied, encrypted, under the new connection's name, the old entry is left as it was, and the step is audited. - **Agent modes are checked.** An alert, a schedule, an integration or an MCP client runs an agent only when the matching agent mode is on. Otherwise the run is refused before the model is called, and recorded with the reason. Agents that were already in use get their mode switched on once, automatically, the first time unattended runs are enabled after the upgrade. Afterwards, check the audit log for `agent_mode_upgrade_conflict` lines: they name agents that need your decision, as the Administrator manual describes. While unattended runs are off, an alert or schedule that fires is now recorded as a refused run instead of being dropped. - **Domain Workspace model edits made before 2.7.0 are assigned or held.** On the first read of a model after the upgrade, Adjutant AI counts the Organisations, the default Organisation included. With exactly one, every earlier edit moves to it. With two or more, the earlier edits are held: users see the model as shipped until an administrator gives each edit to an Organisation or discards it. Nothing is deleted by the upgrade. Afterwards, check the audit log for `workspace_overlay_held` lines and resolve them as the Administrator manual describes (a screen for this follows in a later release). Model edits are now included in the KV Store backup. ### Several sources, one reconciled view (Preview) *Preview.* Staging, acceptance, the reconciliation run and its refusals, approval, promotion and the freshness checks have been run on a live Splunk. Matching records across several sources, and choosing which source wins each field, are tested but have not yet been run live. Most estates describe the same servers, services and teams in more than one place — a CMDB, a monitoring tool, a list a team keeps — and each is partly right. Adjutant AI can now **reconcile** them: read the sources side by side, decide which records are the same thing, and keep one reviewed view in which every value says which source it came from. It is an administrator feature of the **Enterprise** edition and above, driven through the app's REST interface (`/services/itmip_recon`). A run goes through five steps: 1. **Stage** each source's rows into a holding area. 2. **Accept** a source's data as a whole, or reject it as a whole: enough rows, a usable key on every row, no duplicate keys. A read the source reports as **truncated**, or one that lost more rows than the contract allows, is still accepted for what it saw — but it is never used to decide that something is gone. 3. **Reconcile** the accepted data. Every run leaves a record with a verdict — complete, incomplete or refused — and the reason. 4. **Request and approve.** A complete run becomes the approved view only when **a second administrator** approves it. Approving your own request is refused, and who approved is taken from the Splunk session, never from what the request says. 5. **Promote.** The approved run becomes the current view, and the baseline the next run compares against. **It refuses rather than guesses**, and says why: - When a contract names a holding area for its sources, a reconciliation reads only data that was accepted in step 2, and rows sent with the request are refused. - An organisation's first run is reported as a first run. But if the history of an earlier approved run is missing or cannot be read, the run is refused — starting over would give every record a new identity. - If a source's observation time cannot be read, the run is refused rather than using the time the data arrived. - Two contracts never share a run identity, and one organisation's reconciliation never touches another's. - If one record key turns up as two separate records -- typically two sources of the same kind with no matching rule between them -- the run is not complete and cannot be approved, and the run names the contract gap that caused it. **Lookup tables.** A contract can enrich one source's records from up to two lookup tables (for example a region per team). A lookup table never adds a record of its own, each enriched value names the table it came from, and the run reports how much of the table matched nothing. **Renames.** When a record's key changes and nothing else identifies it, reconciliation treats it as a new record. An administrator can record that the two are the same thing (a *rekey*); a second administrator must approve it, and the old record then keeps its history under the new one instead of being reported as gone. **Freshness and trust per source.** Every run records, for each source, whether it was read recently enough and whether it may report that something is gone — each with a named reason when the answer is no. ### Changed: who may approve a blocked integration write - **Only the person who requested a blocked write, or an administrator, may now see, approve or cancel it.** **Power users can no longer approve other users' runs**; ask the requester or an administrator. Publishing writes to a staging name first and promotes it only after the rendered dashboard has been checked, so that a dashboard which fails that check never exists at its real name. That part was right. What was wrong is that a failure to promote still reported success, under the name the dashboard would have had. That happened more than once, and each time the cause was different, so it is worth saying what they had in common rather than listing them as separate faults. The product reaches an AI service by more than one path: the setup checks, the request path through the Splunk server, the browser-direct path, and the scheduled health check. Each had grown its own answer to questions all four have to agree on, and the checks were the path that happened to be right. That is the worst possible arrangement, because the screen a customer is shown passing is not the one serving them. All four now derive the address from one place, and a test compares them across every service and every Azure address shape. It asserts they **agree** rather than asserting any one is correct: a checker that agrees with itself and disagrees with the thing it checks proves nothing. What was actually wrong: * **Gemini did not work through the Splunk server**, which is the only way it can be called. The request went to the stored address, and for Gemini that address is the model list rather than a completion. * **Azure stored as a plain resource address** went to that address instead of to the deployment. * **Azure stored as a complete address** was rebuilt into one URL carrying two deployments, which is what a gateway answered "Resource not found" to. * **A connection with no address stored could not be used at all**, returning *"LLM config has no endpoint stored"* on a connection that had just passed every check. Connections you already saved now work without being re-saved. * **A new connection defaulted to being called from the browser**, and so did one whose call mode had never been recorded. The 2.4.0 reliability work rewrote the retry module in place rather than adding to it, which deleted the LLM call orchestrator — while its one caller, the proxy that **every** Ask goes through, still called it. The result was an `AttributeError` on every request, surfaced as a generic internal error with the real reason only in `splunkd.log`. The orchestrator is restored alongside the newer retry helper. The two are disjoint and stay that way: one is the writer's bounded per-request retry, the other is the provider fallback chain with its circuit breaker and per-attempt journal. `tests/test_llm_retry.py` covers the restored path and was failing on `import` for two releases, which is how this reached a release at all. ### Network-policy events were merged, not split When a device snapshot was stored to a Splunk index, every rule from that device arrived as a **single event** containing the whole batch of JSON records, instead of one event per rule. The same applied to the object, warning and snapshot families. Nothing announced it. The field list still showed `rule_id`, `action`, `source_values` and the rest, because Splunk extracts fields from the first JSON object in an event — so the fields you clicked on were real and correct. Only the **count** was wrong, and the counts the app itself reported were counts of records submitted, not of events landed. A `| stats count by device_id` over the rule source type therefore under-reported by however many rules a device had. The cause was a single character. `default/props.conf` declared the parsing rules under `[adjutant:network_policy:*]`, and props.conf applies its wildcard match language to `source::` and `host::` stanzas only — in a source-type stanza the `*` is literal, so the stanza matched nothing and the events fell back to Splunk's defaults. Each family now has its own stanza, and a `[source::itmip_llm_splunk_writer]` stanza backstops any source type added to that path in future. ### A policy field was colliding with one of Splunk's own Expanded policy tuples carry a field named `source` — and `source` is one of the fields Splunk defines on every event, where it names what wrote the record. Splunk does not overwrite on a collision, it **merges**, so `| table source` returned the policy's source address and `itmip_llm_splunk_writer` together in one cell, with nothing to say which was which. Fields whose names Splunk already owns are now written as `original_` — so that one is `original_source`. This applies to the **index** write only: the KV Store rows, the policy graph and the API keep the model's own names, because `source` is part of what a `tuple_id` is hashed from and renaming it there would move every tuple id ever issued. ### `source` and `host` said who wrote the event, not where the data came from Every network-policy event landed with `source = itmip_llm_splunk_writer` and `host = ai_workbench` — true of every event this app has ever written, and therefore no use for filtering or for a CIM-style view of where a policy came from. They now describe the input. `host` is the box the configuration was **read from**: the device or manager when it was reached over the network, and the Splunk instance itself when the input was a file or a paste, because that is the machine that held it. `source` names the input — a file path when the collector recorded one, else the file name, else `cisco:asa:config` for a device configuration or `cisco:fmc:api` for a manager collection. An FMC collection is labelled by the **manager**, not by the device platform it describes, which is the distinction the field is for. ### An Org with its own mapping collection saw an empty one — or someone else's An Org that registers a `mapping_collection` gets its own (`itmip_ai_mappings_`), which is the isolation boundary. The shipped example mappings were only ever seeded into `DFLT`'s, so that collection stayed **empty**: the examples were invisible to the Org, and an integration resolving its `mapping_ref` at run time under that Org found nothing. Compounding it, the Mappings tab did not tell the server which app it was in, so it resolved as the fallback Org and displayed **DFLT's** collection. An admin could Verify and Clear a mapping there, and a schedule running under their real Org would still refuse — pointing at a row in a collection nobody was looking at. The shipped examples are now seeded per Org, and the tab resolves the same Org the runtime does. **One consequence to know about:** mappings authored while the tab was mis-resolving live in the fallback Org's collection. They are not lost, but they belong to that Org and will not appear under yours. Re-create or re-scope anything you need. ### Seeded mappings could never be corrected after the first install A seeded mapping is documented as re-seed-eligible: ship a fix, and an untouched system-owned row picks it up. It never worked. The seeder POSTed to the KV Store collection root, which only ever **inserts** — splunkd answers `409` for a `_key` that already exists and leaves the row alone — and the 409 landed in a bare `except: pass`. Every correction to a shipped mapping since the first install was silently dropped. A second guard compounded it: the seeder skipped any row cleared for unattended use. That was added for a real reason (restarts were resetting clearance) but it froze the whole row rather than the decision, so the mapping most likely to run unattended was the one fixes could never reach. On a real instance the shipped Cisco ASA mapping was still at its pre-B3.3 shape: **no `device_id` in the projection** and **no `source.schema_version`**, so the writer's schema pin had nothing to compare and could not refuse a batch the mapping would silently strip of its NAT view. The refusal that exists to prevent exactly that could not fire. Now: the seeder replaces then inserts, so corrections land; and clearance is carried across an unchanged re-seed but **revoked when the content actually changed**, recording who had cleared it and why it was revoked. A human cleared a specific mapping, not a name — so a changed mapping stops and asks, instead of running under an approval that no longer describes it. ### The shipped ASA Playbook pointed at a superseded mapping "Cisco ASA Policy Ingestion (mapping-driven)" was wired to `cisco-asa-config-to-network-policy-v1`, which is `superseded_by` v2 and pinned to source schema 1.0. The pipeline has emitted 2.0 since the NAT work, so a run through it is refused with `schema_version_mismatch` — and the refusal names v2, meaning the product was telling operators to fix a wiring mistake the product shipped with. The Playbook now names v2. The trailing `-v1` / `-v2` in a mapping name is its **schema generation**, not its lifecycle version; a mapping carries its own `operational v1` separately. Two axes, one letter. The Playbook's mapping picker now shows each mapping's title alongside its ref (the Mappings tab lists them by title, so the same mapping looked like two different objects), flags a superseded choice with the successor's name before you save, and spells out that clearing for unattended is a separate step from promoting. ### Policy records were stamped with the wrong Org and BU Run a network-policy ingestion from the Ask tab in a host app such as `itmip_fis_app`, with the header showing your real Org and BU, and every landed record still said `tenant_org: DFLT`, `tenant_bu: DFLT`. Org and BU are resolved server-side from the caller's roles **and** the app they are working in. The Ask request itself sends that app; the tool dispatch behind it did not, so resolution fell back to the assistant app's own name — which matches whichever Org registered *that* pattern, not the one the user is in. An Org whose `app_patterns` name the host app could never match. The netpol, `splunk_memory` and `splunk_mapping` tool calls now send the host app. This is a context hint, not a grant — an Org matches only when the caller's real roles also match its `role_patterns` — so it cannot widen anyone's access; it makes tenant data land under the tenant it belongs to. Records written on 2.4.0 or 2.4.1 through these tools carry the fallback Org/BU and are not corrected retroactively. **This one is in the frontend bundle**, so hard-refresh the browser after upgrading. ### Security: raw firewall configurations were readable by every authenticated user `itmip_netpol_artifacts` stores collected configurations as base64. Redaction on the import path is opt-in, so unless it was asked for, a stored artifact still contains the secrets the scanner merely counted — on our own sample config, an enable-password hash and two IKEv2 pre-shared keys. That collection had no ACL of its own, so it inherited the app default of `read : [ * ]`. Every protection the artifact store provides — tenant scoping, an owner check, metadata-only reads, a download link that expires in an hour — guards the REST path; a direct KV Store read from a lookup command or the Lookup Editor went around all of it. `itmip_netpol_artifacts`, `itmip_netpol_parses` and `itmip_netpol_snapshots` are now **admin / sc_admin** read and write. No functional change: every netpol read goes through the endpoint's system token, and that endpoint was already admin-gated. The published policy collections (`itmip_network_policy_rules_current` and its siblings) stay readable — they hold modelled policy rather than credentials, and searching them is the product. **If you have run a collection on 2.4.0 or 2.4.1**, treat any credential in a collected config as having been readable by any app user for the artifact's 7-day retention, and rotate accordingly. ### Warnings you can trace back to what they are about A network-policy warning carried `code`, `message` and `line` — a sentence, and no way to go and look. `line` also answers nothing for an API collection, which has objects rather than lines. Warning events now carry `refs{}` (the ACL name, the object id, the uuid an FMC rule referenced — identifiers the parser had already collected and the index write was discarding), `evidence_ref` in the same `#L` form that rules use for `raw_evidence_refs`, and `artifact_id`. One idiom now locates a warning and a rule alike. The offending configuration line itself is still never carried into an index — it stays in the protected, secret-scanned artifact, and the evidence ref is how you reach it. ### Duplicate warnings on the same collection Warnings from an FMC collection are built per rule side, so two access rules referencing the same uncollected port object produced the same warning twice — and the indexed warning event carries `code`, `message` and `line` and nothing else, so the copies were indistinguishable and the repetition told you nothing. Byte-identical warnings now collapse to one; anything that differs, even by a line number, is still two warnings. On a busy or delayed pipeline that moves events on the timeline. One stanza per OCSF class now. **Upgrading.** These are index-time settings: they apply to events indexed **after** a splunkd restart, and events already in the index stay merged. To correct history, remove the affected events and re-store the snapshots. --- ## 2.4.1 "Getting connected" Everything here came out of two customer setups in the same fortnight: an Azure OpenAI service published through a corporate API gateway, and one behind a private endpoint. The release is about closing the distance between "the test passes" and "it works", and about not making an administrator assemble a URL by hand from three values nobody gave them. ### Find my endpoint (Azure OpenAI) Azure needs the complete address of a deployment, not the address of the service: everything up to and including `/chat/completions`, with the deployment name and an api-version in it. Behind a gateway that address also carries a path prefix chosen by whoever publishes the API. An administrator is typically handed a base URL and expected to work out the other three parts, and getting any of them wrong produces a "Resource not found" that reads like a permissions problem. There is now a **Find my endpoint** button beneath the endpoint field. Give it whatever you were given — often just the hostname — and it works out the rest from the Splunk server itself, then offers to fill in the endpoint, the deployment and the api-version in one click. It finds the address by paying attention to *how* each attempt is refused rather than just that it failed. A gateway refusing an address it does not publish answers differently from Azure refusing a deployment name it does not have, and the second kind of refusal proves the rest of the address is already right. When it cannot finish the job it says exactly what is still missing instead of failing vaguely — most usefully "the address and version are confirmed, the deployment name is not", which turns a five-part question for the API team into a one-part question. It checked whether the credential was accepted, and an address that answers "not found" still accepts a credential — so a wrong address passed the test and failed every time it was used. The licence page now says the key was issued without a device limit and needs reissuing, instead of sending administrators round a loop that had no exit. --- ## 2.2.2 "Finish the dashboard" A maintenance release about one thing: runs that did all the work and then ended with nothing on the glass. It is the layer above them that finds what they miss across channels, connects the entities they cannot, and turns three weeks of investigation into an afternoon with a trail you can hand to an auditor. ## 2.0.7 "Memory, Scheduled Ask & Integrations" Adjutant AI gains a durable memory, a scheduled/unattended surface, and a governed data-integration subsystem — so it stops re-asking, can run on a clock, and can sync a system of record into Splunk under a contract two humans have reviewed. - **Memory — it stops re-asking.** A small, durable, per-tenant memory: **learned facts** (the index a report uses, what "the Cribl search" means for a team) captured the moment they're learned, and **integration watermarks**.
