If you have never enabled it, nothing changes for you. **Fixed** - **A run that keeps failing now gives up instead of restarting forever.** If a background run died, it was put back in the queue and started again — without counting how many times it had already failed. A run that failed every time (a bad playbook, a bug) could restart indefinitely and keep occupying a worker. Runs are now retried a set number of times and then parked as "given up", where they stop consuming anything and wait for a person. - **The per-run time limit now actually applies.** The "maximum time for one run" setting was shown in the configuration, charted on the dashboard and alerted on — but nothing enforced it. Runs now stop when they reach it. - **A stuck run is stopped, not just forgotten.** Previously the engine handed the work to a new run but left the stuck one alive, so two runs could work on the same alert and both spend money. The stuck one is now stopped first. - **Long, healthy runs are no longer interrupted.** A slow-but-fine run could be mistaken for a dead one and restarted underneath itself. Runs now report that they are alive continuously rather than only between steps. **New** - **Limits that protect Splunk itself.** A background run now caps its own memory, CPU and priority, so a runaway run degrades into one failed investigation instead of putting the Splunk platform under pressure. Sensible defaults are set for you; all are adjustable, and each can be switched off. - **You can now see stuck and given-up runs.** A run only reports on itself when it finishes, so runs that got stuck were invisible on every dashboard. The *Pipeline Knobs* dashboard has a new run-health section (stuck runs, given-up runs, runs being retried, and what each worker is doing), and two new optional alerts — **Runner stuck** and **Runs dead-lettered** — tell you without anyone having to look. Both are off by default. **Changed** - The retry setting is now called **`runner_max_attempts`** (it covers every kind of failure, not only runaway runs). The unused `retain_completed_hours` setting has been removed — run history retention is controlled by `queue_retention`. If you set either in a local override, update it. --- ## 1.8.5 "CIM Coverage Audit" When a data source is onboarded but a correlation search in Enterprise Security still comes back empty, or an ITSI KPI never fills, the cause is almost always that the source is not properly mapped to the CIM data model the search depends on. Finding out why is normally a slow, manual walk through the layers. The CIM Coverage Audit does it for you, from your real events and your real search head configuration. **New** - **Audit a sourcetype against a CIM dataset.** Ask, for example, audit cisco:asa against the Network Traffic All_Traffic dataset. You get back how much of the dataset the source covers, and if it does not, which layer is broken: the source is not tagged so the model cannot see it, its index is not on the model's allowlist, a field is missing or under the wrong name, a value needs normalizing, or the accelerated summaries the correlation searches read have not caught up. That last one is the confusing case where CIM works when you test it by hand but your correlation searches fire nothing, and the audit calls it out plainly. - **A fix you can read and deploy.** For each gap the audit produces the exact configuration, checked for validity, shown as your current stanza next to the proposed one, with a note on where it belongs. It never deploys anything itself. You review and apply it, which is what lets you run this where an automatic write to production would never pass change control. - **Honest about what a search head can see.** Adjutant AI runs on the search head, so it reads your search time configuration and the real events, and it is upfront that it cannot read the index time configuration on your indexers. It runs its searches as you, so it can never read data from an index you could not otherwise search. - Three read only helpers to read a sourcetype's search head props and transforms and check where a sourcetype has data. The diagnosis is available on Professional so any platform team can see which layer is broken. Generating the validated fix is an Enterprise feature. It grades against the CIM add on actually installed on your search head. Restart Splunk after upgrading. **Fixed** - **The app opens on the Ask tab again.** If your LLM runs entirely on the search head, with the key held server side (the Splunk proxy mode, an Azure managed identity, or a Bedrock role), the browser never receives an API key. The app used to read that as nothing being configured and jumped to the Settings tab on every launch. It now opens on Ask as intended, and only sends you to Settings when a key really is needed and missing. - **Clearer license status.** When a license is installed but the app cannot confirm it is active on this environment, it now tells you that directly instead of quietly dropping to the free Personal tier. Admins get a pointer to the License page to re-activate. --- ## 1.8.4 "Async playbooks over MCP" Run Adjutant AI playbooks from an AI agent over the Model Context Protocol with a reliable **start → poll → fetch** pattern. A playbook can take several minutes, but AI tool calls are subject to short timeouts you don't control (the MCP server, the client, proxies), so trying to wait for the answer in one call is fragile. Now every call returns in seconds. **New / Improved** - **Start returns immediately.** `adjutantai_start_playbook` (the old `adjutantai_run_playbook` name is removed) hands back a run id at once with a hint on how to poll. - **Check progress** with `adjutantai_get_playbook_status` — queued, running, completed, or failed (a run that hit a recoverable error and is auto‑retrying is reported as still running, not failed), with guidance to stop polling after ~15 minutes. - **Fetch the verdict** with `adjutantai_get_playbook_results` once completed — condensed by default, or the full result on request; a partial result is clearly labelled. - **Tenant‑safe.** One team can't read another team's run; unknown or expired run ids simply return "not found." Run records are kept for 7 days by default. - **Try it out of the box:** start `MCP Example: Read-only Health Check` under Org/BU `DFLT/DFLT` (the read‑only reference playbook shipped on every install), then poll and fetch. Requires the inbound MCP server and the Backend Ask Service to be enabled. No configuration changes. Restart Splunk after upgrading. ### Also in 1.8.4 — the Outcome Ledger (Enterprise) A single screen that answers what a CEO, CISO or auditor actually asks: *what did agentic AI do for us this period, was it any good, what did it save, what did it cost — and can I see the evidence for one run?* It assembles data the app already records (unattended‑run history, analyst agreement, run telemetry, LLM spend) into one executive/audit view. It adds **no new data collection and sends nothing to any external service.** **New** - **The dashboard** (`Adjutant AI ▸ Outcome Ledger`): headline tiles (investigations run without a human, how often analysts agreed with the AI — with the sample size and coverage shown, benign/false‑positive runs auto‑closed, analyst hours saved, LLM spend, typical time to a verdict), the mix of AI conclusions over time, agreement by case type, a weekly ledger, and an **evidence** table you can click through to the full detail of any single run. A footer spells out every assumption so a number is never quoted out of context. - **Safe to hand to an auditor.** What each viewer may see is decided on the server from their own identity — never from the page — and fails closed. In this release the dashboard is for Splunk administrators; scoped, delegated auditor access is the next step. - **Is the AI real, or just performing?** An Efficacy Trend panel puts run volume against how often analysts agreed, over time. If the agent runs more while analysts increasingly override it, the panel says so ("scaling faster than trust") instead of hiding it behind a healthy‑looking headline — and on too little feedback it honestly says the sample is too thin to judge. - **Honest numbers.** Effort saved is shown as time (with the per‑case assumption stated), spend is the real logged cost, and the per‑investigation efficiency signal is token usage — never an invented cost estimate. Enterprise feature. No effect on any existing behaviour. Restart Splunk after upgrading. --- ## 1.8.3 "Security hardening" A security‑focused release. Adjutant AI was put through an independent OWASP Top 10 (web **and** LLM), dependency‑vulnerability, and "AI‑driven ransomware" review. The headline: **no critical issues, no default passwords or keys, no vulnerable components that ship to you, and the assistant cannot be turned into an attack tool.** Confirmed issues are fixed; a plain‑language, reviewer‑ready write‑up ships in the app as `SECURITY_AUDIT.md`. **Improved / Fixed** - **Credentials stay server‑side.** Provider API keys and keyless Azure sign‑in secrets are never sent to the browser or to other users in your tenant. (The free‑tier browser API‑key path is unchanged.) - **Prompts stay in your audit index**, not Splunk's internal logs. - **Stronger multi‑tenant isolation** for investigation results and knowledge sources. - **You confirm every change.** Closing a notable, setting a disposition, an ITSI/TrackMe/ServiceNow write, or overwriting a saved dashboard now asks for explicit confirmation first. Read‑only questions and new private dashboards are unaffected. - **General hardening:** cleaner errors, tighter sign‑in redirects, safer content‑pack imports, email TLS verification on by default. No new features or config changes. Restart Splunk after upgrading. --- ## 1.8.2 "Edge Processor data-quality + keyless Azure OpenAI auth" **Keyless Azure OpenAI (Microsoft Entra ID / managed identity).** Connect Azure OpenAI **without a static API key** — using a Microsoft Entra ID service principal or a managed identity, governed by your Entra tenant. Runs entirely server-side (no token reaches the browser), supports Public and US Gov clouds, and adds a one-click **Test connection** that names exactly what to fix if something is off. Connecting Azure with a plain **API key** still works on every tier; the keyless Entra path is an **Enterprise** capability. --- ### Edge Processor data-quality If your data passes through **Splunk Edge Processor** before it reaches Splunk, some parsing, timestamping, dropping and routing happens *upstream* — where Splunk's own internal logs and feed-health tools can't see it. This release teaches the assistant to look at that hop. - **New "Edge Processor → Splunk data-quality check".** Ask the assistant to check an Edge Processor feed and it reads Edge Processor's own operational metrics (throughput, dropped events, failed destination sends, and queue backpressure) and tells you, in plain language, whether data is being silently lost or delayed before it lands — with a proof dashboard. - **Honest by design.** If Edge Processor telemetry isn't reaching your Splunk yet, the assistant says so and gives you the exact setup steps (on-premises vs Splunk Cloud) instead of inventing a clean bill of health. It reports at the pipeline level and is clear that per-event checks need a small addition to your Edge Processor pipeline. - **Folds into the readiness verdict.** Edge Processor joins Splunk parsing, feed-health, and Cribl as another "is this data actually good?" signal, and can cap the Data Quality Score when it finds upstream loss. - Read-only and available on every tier, exactly like the existing Cribl check. --- ## 1.8.1 "Cleaner support diagnosis" A small maintenance update over 1.8.0 (front-end only). - **More accurate "Report an issue" diagnosis.** The automated issue classifier no longer mislabels a session that finished normally — one that completed and produced its dashboard — as having "run out of tool steps." The suspected-issue summary in your support bundle is now cleaner for healthy, tool-heavy sessions. --- ## 1.8.0 "Agent telemetry & OCSF export, content packs & all-tiers data quality" **New — your SOC can watch the agent (OCSF telemetry).** - **Adjutant AI emits its own activity as OCSF.** Every LLM call, tool / MCP / ServiceNow call, configuration change, unattended run verdict, and **policy refusal** (the proof the controls actually fire) can be written as open-standard **OCSF** events to a Splunk index your Enterprise Security / SOC already watches — mapped to CIM via the community **OCSF-CIM Add-On**. Your SOC monitors our agent the same way it monitors everything else: on-prem, with no cloud egress. - **You stay in control.** It is **off by default** and Enterprise-gated. **You provision and name the index** (the app ships no `indexes.conf`). Routing and content are resolved **per Organisation / Business Unit**; content export is denied by default and never exceeds your audit (DPIA) ceiling, with a server-side redaction check before anything is written. - **See it immediately.** A shipped admin dashboard — *Adjutant AI — Behaviour (OCSF)* — shows the token trend, model mix, tool/MCP egress with identity, the refusal and finding feeds, and a per-run drilldown, all on raw OCSF (no CIM Add-On required). **New — update Adjutant's content without waiting for a whole new app release.** - **Content packs.** Almost everything Adjutant does well lives in its **content** — the skills, knowledge, and playbooks. A **content pack** is a single, versioned file that lets us ship a corrected or improved content set straight to your install, and lets your admin apply it safely — no Splunkbase re-vetting cycle for a content fix. - **Your changes are protected.** Applying a pack **upgrades only the items you haven't changed**. Anything your team has customised is left exactly as-is and clearly listed, never silently overwritten — and your Org/BU scoping is always preserved. After an import you get a per-item report, and the list of items that need manual reconciliation is downloadable as a CSV. - **Safe by design.** Every pack carries an integrity check, so a tampered or truncated file is refused. Imports live on the **Backups** page, which also shows which content version you're currently on — run a backup first and you can roll back in one click. - **Retire without deleting.** A pack can mark an item **retired** — it stays installed but is hidden and switched off everywhere (it can't be picked, run, or used by the assistant). An admin can re-enable it at any time by removing the tag. **Improved — data-quality checks for everyone, and Splunk 10.x readiness.** - **Data-quality ingestion checks are now available on every edition, including the free tier.** Checking whether a feed is actually landing and parsing correctly — on `index=_internal`, through **TrackMe**, and through **Cribl Stream** — is a baseline capability now, not a Professional add-on. - **Ready for Splunk Enterprise 10.2 and 10.4.** The app declares Python 3.9 **and** 3.13 compatibility and has been audited against the 10.x platform changes (dashboards, the web framework, KV Store). Your admin still completes the standard KV Store engine migration as part of any 10.x upgrade. - **Smarter Dashboard Studio building.** The assistant now works from a single, version-aware map of what Dashboard Studio supports on **your** Splunk version — it won't reach for a chart type your version can't render, and when your Splunk is newer than what we've documented it builds conservatively and verifies the result. **Fixed.** - **Fewer false "the dashboard is blank" errors.** A heavy Dashboard Studio dashboard that renders fine but slowly is no longer wrongly reported as blank — the assistant confirms the panels actually returned data before deciding, so it stops wasting a retry on a dashboard that was already correct. A genuinely blank dashboard is still caught. - **TrackMe panels only when they belong.** Fixed a rule that pushed a TrackMe feed-health panel onto every generated dashboard (and used a lookup that fails outside the TrackMe app). The assistant now adds a feed-health panel only when it's actually relevant, using a method that works in your app. --- ## 1.7.0 "ServiceNow integration" (included in the 1.8.0 release) > **Renamed to Adjutant AI.** The app is now **Adjutant AI** (formerly "AI Workbench"). > This is a **display-name change only** — the in-app title (the easter egg now lives on > the dot of the "i" in **Adjutant Ai**), the app label, the documentation, and the > assistant's own self-description all say **Adjutant AI**. Nothing functional changed: > the Splunk app id, your saved searches/dashboards/models, KVStore data, and generated > artifact names are unchanged, so the upgrade is seamless. **New — run playbooks automatically, and from other Splunk apps.** - **On a schedule or on an event.** A playbook can run **unattended** on a schedule (a "morning health check") or in response to a Splunk event — an alert, an ES correlation search, or an ITSI episode. When an event triggers it, the affected thing (the host, user, or entity in the alert) is handed to the playbook automatically, so it investigates exactly what fired. Two ready-made (disabled) examples are included to copy. - **Adjutant AI as a building block for other apps.** Other Splunk AI agents can now ask Adjutant AI to **list** and **run** your playbooks through a small, safe interface (an MCP server). Only playbooks you mark **MCPready** are exposed, every call must name the Org/BU it is for (which must be a business unit you have set up) as a safeguard, and runs go through the same governed, bounded service — never an open door. This interface is **off by default** — turn it on with one setting. When on, the tools can also appear inside **Splunk's own MCP Server**, reachable on the normal Splunk web address (no special port needed); you authenticate with a standard Splunk token. A ready-made, read-only **example playbook** ships enabled so there is always something to see the moment you switch the interface on. **New — "Report an issue" support packaging (all editions).** - One click on any conversation (per-turn 🐞, the Ask panel, or the new **Help tab**) packages exactly what happened — versions, the resolved prompt, the tools and model used, the generated dashboards/searches, and every error and warning — into a single file. - **Safe by construction:** secrets are stripped before anything leaves the browser, and the file is **encrypted** to the support key, so it's safe to send over any channel. - It even **tells you what kind of problem it looks like** and matches known issues, so simple cases are solved without a back-and-forth. - **Send it your way:** download it and attach it to your own ticket, use the built-in support form, or email it. The **Help tab** (Report + Documentation + About) is always reachable — even if the app is locked by licensing. **New — ServiceNow, done properly** (Professional + the `servicenow` feature). Read incidents, changes, problems and the **CMDB/CSDM** in plain English — with bounded blast-radius / dependency traversals ("what's the blast radius if this CI fails?"). Turn a Splunk alert, ITSI episode or ES notable into a rich, deterministically rendered ServiceNow incident and **write the number back** to the originating object (a re-fire updates, never duplicates; the closed-incident policy is configurable). **Security incidents (SIR)** with MITRE ATT&CK, off until an admin enables them. Two transports (REST **or** a ServiceNow MCP server), plus TISC threat-intel enrichment — all server-side and allowlisted, so ServiceNow can never block the assistant. *(Verified against the documented APIs and unit-tested; final certification is on a live ServiceNow.)* **New — run playbooks automatically, and from other apps.** Playbooks can run **unattended** on a schedule, or from a Splunk alert / ES correlation search / ITSI episode (the triggering entity is handed to the run). Adjutant AI can also expose **list / run** over an inbound **MCP server** (off by default, MCPready-only, Org/BU-scoped) — reachable inside Splunk's own MCP Server on the normal web address, with a standard Splunk token. **New — "Report an issue" support packaging (all editions).** One click packages a failing conversation — secret-stripped and **encrypted client-side** — with an automatic problem classification, plus an always-reachable **Help tab** even when the app is licence-locked. **New — Cribl Stream data-quality awareness** (Professional+). Reads Cribl's own forwarded logs and metrics to surface the timestamp / parse / dropped-event problems that happen *inside Cribl, before Splunk can see them* — the "green in Splunk but timestamped wrong" blind spot — folded into one readiness verdict. No Cribl Lake or Search required. **New — LLM reliability: retry, fallback & circuit breaker** (Enterprise). A brief provider hiccup (503 / 529 / rate-limit) auto-retries within a time budget; a per-config **circuit breaker** stops hammering a provider that's down, then probes for recovery; and an ordered **fallback** transparently switches to your next provider (and tells you which it used). Two new admin dashboards — **LLM Health** and **AI Activity** — plus per-user / BU / org concurrency caps, all conservative and off the critical path. **New — live model & cost catalogue (all editions).** Models and prices come from a runtime catalogue that updates without an app rebuild; **automatic model discovery** (Professional+) keeps it current without ever logging your keys; an Enterprise admin screen adds price overrides and manual model registration for private gateways. **Fixed.** Generated Simple XML dashboards now share a single base search across panels (faster) and get a top data-ingestion health panel; corrected a 3× Opus price over-charge (now server-side authoritative, with Opus 4.8 and Fable 5 included). --- ## 1.5.0 "Data Foundation & MCP OAuth" **New:** connect to **OAuth 2.1‑protected MCP servers** (authorization‑code + PKCE for interactive, client‑credentials for unattended; tokens held server‑side, never in the browser — see [MCP_OAUTH.md](MCP_OAUTH.md)); **onboard new data sources** — describe a source or attach a sample file and get a deployment‑ready add‑on package; a **"is my data parsed correctly?"** ingestion/timestamp check that reads Splunk's own internal logs; generated config **validated against your instance** and given a **0–100 Data Quality Score** (A–F); and attach a local sample file in Ask (only the file name is audited, never contents). **Improved:** works with the newest OpenAI "reasoning" models incl. Azure GPT‑5.4 / GPT‑5.4‑mini (auto‑detects the request format); more reliable generated dashboards; generated objects use the **`aiworkbench`** name tag; and Audit‑tab improvements (Business Unit column/filter, local‑timezone timestamps, reliable token/outcome capture). --- ## Earlier releases (1.0.0 – 1.4.3) - **1.4.3** — Clearer guidance and plain-language fixes when a free-tier LLM key hits its provider limits (e.g. Groq token-per-minute caps, Gemini zero-quota keys); the LLM config screen flags these up front. - **1.4.1** — Per-feature capability licensing with edition badges (Professional / Enterprise / MSP); gated features show a padlock, and nothing you created is ever deleted when a tier changes. Turn-level audit logging made reliable; more robust dashboard generation. - **1.4.0** — The assistant reads your own Splunk **live** (real search commands + installed visualizations) instead of guessing; Splunk Security Essentials detection content integrated. - **1.3.3** — TrackMe integration end-to-end (feed-health awareness + actions) with richer built-in platform knowledge. - **1.3.2** — First Splunkbase 1.x release: packaging and permissions hardening. - **1.3.1** — Fixed Org/BU edits dropping fields; safeguard to keep bundled playbooks correct after upgrades. - **1.3.0** — Real, per-Organisation audit logging of every AI interaction (Professional+). - **1.2.0** — Splunk Security Essentials content tools for playbooks. - **1.1.1** — Cisco Deep Time Series Model (CDTSM) playbooks: pre-trained anomaly detection and forecasting via the AI Toolkit, each with a proof dashboard. - **1.1.0** — Multi-tenancy and the Organisation / Business-Unit editor overhauled for clearer, safer tenant scoping. - **1.0.0** — The knowledge layer: ground answers in your organisation's own conventions. *(Releases before 1.0 are early pre-release history and are omitted here.)* --- ## Known issues - **Open the assistant from inside another app.** Adjutant AI is a "host shell": reach it from a navigation-menu entry inside Search, Enterprise Security, ITSI, or your own apps — not by clicking the app tile directly. Everything it creates lands in the namespace of the app you opened it from. - **Some Data Foundation features need self-hosted Splunk.** The configuration-reference grounding and config-package generation (1.5.0) read files on the Splunk server, so they are unavailable on Splunk Cloud; the assistant says so and continues with what it can. --- *When a published fix resolves a tracked GitHub issue, it is summarised here with its issue number — for example: "Fixed: a dashboard panel could display raw HTML markup as text instead of formatting it (#123)."*


Short Description:
Your Splunk experts stop being the queue. Ask in plain words, and governed AI agents build working searches, dashboards and alerts, and can start investigating the moment an alert, ES notable or ITSI episode fires. Every step shown live, every action gated. Your keys stay on your side, and your data goes to no model but the one you choose. Free for one user.


Description:
Every Splunk team has the same bottleneck: a handful of people who write SPL, and a queue of everyone else. Adjutant AI turns that queue into agents. - Describe what you need in plain words and get a real search, dashboard or alert. The agent tests it before it saves it, and you own it. - Alerts, Enterprise Security notables and ITSI episodes are investigated by an agent before anyone opens them, once you switch it on. - You watch every step live and can stop it at any time. Every action is gated, and on Enterprise every run is audited. Each agent works with the asking person's own Splunk permissions, on the LLM you choose, on Splunk Enterprise or Splunk Cloud. One app on your search head serves Search, Enterprise Security, ITSI and your own apps. Depending on your edition, agents also work with the AI Toolkit, TrackMe, ServiceNow, your own HTTP tools and other MCP servers, and other AI agents can use yours as tools through MCP. Your keys stay on your side, and your data goes to no model but the one you choose. Free for one user to build searches, dashboards and alerts, with no licence key needed.

item.title: Forcepoint Insights SIEM App - v1.1.2 [New App Release]
item.description:
Platform: Splunk


Release Notes:
**Release 1.1.2** **What's new** * **Proxy settings in separate fields.** The single Proxy text box on the setup page is now five fields: Scheme, Host, Port, Username and Password. They sit in a collapsible Proxy section. The app builds the proxy URL itself, so special characters in a password, such as `@` or `:`, now work correctly. * **Stricter proxy checks.** Proxy settings are checked when you save, both in the browser and on the server. Hosts that are badly formed or ambiguous are rejected, and so are IPv6 addresses that aren't closed properly. A pasted URL such as [`http://proxy.example.com:8080`](http://proxy.example.com:8080) in the Host field is split into Scheme, Host and Port automatically. * **Readable collection names.** The setup page now shows each collection's display name. This only changes what the page shows: stored settings and exported data are unchanged. **Security fixes** * The setup page no longer shows a saved proxy password. It appears as `********`. * Proxy credentials are now stored as separate entries in Splunk's encrypted credential store, instead of inside a proxy URL. * Proxy credentials and the API key no longer appear in error messages on the setup page, or in `splunkd.log` at the default log level. **Bug fixes** * Setup errors are now specific instead of a generic "Something went wrong". The page tells proxy, TLS, timeout, connection and authentication failures apart, and shows each one under the field it relates to. * An invalid API key (HTTP 401/403) is now reported against the API Key field. * A proxy that can't be reached now fails within seconds instead of leaving the setup page waiting. * You can now remove a configured proxy by clearing its fields. Before, saving failed, and the error pointed at the wrong field. **Upgrading** * Your existing proxy configuration keeps working after the upgrade, with no changes needed. The next time you open and save the setup page, the old setting is converted to the new fields automatically. * No changes to collections, exported fields, saved export progress or log format. Data is not fetched again. * If you save the setup page on 1.1.2 and then downgrade to 1.1.1 or earlier, you will need to enter the proxy again on the older version.


Description:
The Forcepoint Insights SIEM App for Splunk delivers centralized visibility into Forcepoint security logs, including Forcepoint ONE SSE and Cloud Web Security, with prebuilt dashboards, searches, and analytics to accelerate threat detection, compliance, and incident response. Administrators can selectively configure which products and data collections are exported through the app for a flexible and scalable SIEM integration experience.

item.title: Input Add On for SentinelOne App For Splunk - v7.0.0 [Version Update]
item.description:
Platform: Splunk


Release Notes:
\## CIM 8.6 Compliance \- Exported the full CIM knowledge-object chain (props, transforms, lookups, eventtypes, tags) system-wide so Splunk Enterprise Security and Search & Reporting can resolve tags outside the app context (metadata/default.meta). \- Fixed hardcoded index\=main in the sentinelone_base_index eventtype — replaced with "index\=\* sourcetype\=sentinelone:\*" so customers using custom indexes get CIM tags correctly. \- Added UAM Unified Alerts to the CIM Alerts data model (sentinelone:channel:uam_alerts and sentinelone:channel:uam_alerts:createdAt). Includes id, type, severity, severity_id, app, dest, src, user, signature, and storyline field mappings. \- Fixed the FIELDALIAS_threatinfo_storyline typo (underscore to dash) — the storyline field now correctly appears on sentinelone:channel:threats events. \- Added severity_id (numeric, CIM 8.6 required) to threats, UAM alerts, and vulnerability sourcetypes. \- False-positive threats now map to severity\=informational (previously they remained at critical/medium). \- Fixed the type field on threats — now emits CIM-valid "alert" instead of static/dynamic; raw detection type preserved in s1_detection_type. \- Split the Change data model: genuine account / identity lifecycle events (user and service-user create/modify/delete, RBAC roles, API-token access, credential/2FA/password management, account lockouts) now route to Account_Management only via the new sentinelone_change_account eventtype; all other activities route to Auditing_Changes only. Membership uses an explicit activityType ID allowlist (not the lookup's change_type column, which name-heuristically tags many non-lifecycle "User ..." operations) so unrelated events such as endpoint quarantine, CVE/scan actions, script approvals and AD operations are not misclassified into Account_Management. The dashboard, the saved search, and the report's acceleration section now accept either form. \- **\*\*Run times without \`\_internal\`\*\*** -- Avg Run and P90 Run on the Data Model Health tab and in \`cim_validator_acceleration_health\` came from a 7-day search of \`index\=\_internal\` scheduler logs, which is empty for users without access to that index (common on managed ES search heads). They now read \`summary.average_time\` and \`summary.p90\` from the summarization endpoint, which Splunk maintains for every accelerated model, so the columns fill for anyone who can open the tab. N/A appears only when Splunk has not recorded a run yet. \- **\*\*TA Inventory view\*\*** -- New view (menu bar: TA Inventory) with four exportable tables. Observed CIM Coverage lists every sourcetype with events in a CIM data model, with its models, indexes, and tags, read from the summary index so it is instant. Configured CIM Coverage walks eventtypes, tags, props, and CIM data model constraints through REST to show which add-ons are configured to normalize which sourcetypes into which models, with events seen in range (0 means configured but no data). Sourcetypes Missing from Inventory lists mapped sourcetypes absent from \`cim_sourcetype_inventory\`. Installed Splunk Apps mirrors Manage Apps (name, folder, version, update checking, visibility, sharing, status, derived app origin, update available) for sharing with a CIM reviewer. \- **\*\*Collection writes observed tags\*\*** -- Each dataset job now also records the CIM tags carried by every index/sourcetype as one \`ReportType\=cim_observed_tags\` row per model/dataset/index/sourcetype. No new search jobs; the tags ride along in the existing \`tstats\`. The dashboard base search filters on \`cim_validator_v2\`, so existing panels and the report are unaffected. The Observed table fills after the first collection run on 2.12.1. \- **\*\*Data model retention reads the effective value\*\*** -- Retention (days) on the Data Model Health tab and in \`cim_validator_acceleration_health\` came from \`/services/data/models\`, which returns one row per \`datamodels.conf\` layer; with two apps setting \`acceleration.earliest_time\` the panel showed whichever row came first. It now uses the summarization endpoint's effective range, falling back to the merged \`conf-datamodels\` value, and a new Retention Conflict column lists every app and value when layers disagree. \- **\*\*Tier markers in Data Model Test SPL\*\*** -- The Generated SPL places \`REQ\`, \`REC\`, and \`OPT\` marker columns in front of the Required, Recommended, and Optional field groups so a reviewer can see where each tier begins. Only tiers with fields get a marker. Suggested by NS2 Security Ops during a CAT walkthrough. **v2.11.1 (October 20, 2026)** \- **\*\*Scope filter honors sourcetype inventory\*\*** -- The quality KPIs, the CIM Compliance tab, the Remediation Priorities tab, and the automated report filtered by data model category only, so a sourcetype the inventory marks operational (for example \`snow:sysevents\`, mapped to Change, whose category is security and operational) counted under the Security scope. All of them now also check the sourcetype's inventory scope; only sourcetypes missing from the inventory fall back to the model category. \- **\*\*Exclusions report enriched\*\*** -- \`cim_sourcetype_exclusions_search\` now joins each excluded sourcetype to \`cim_sourcetype_inventory\` (tech category, scope, security relevance, data models, vendor, description, expanded description, provenance) so exclusions can be reviewed in context. Sourcetypes missing from the inventory still appear with blank enrichment columns. \- **\*\*CIM Coverage honors sourcetype inventory\*\*** -- The CIM Coverage KPI, its daily trend collection, and the report counted a sourcetype as mapped only when it mapped to a model in the selected scope's category, so a security sourcetype mapped only to an operational model counted as unmapped and the KPI disagreed with the Unmapped Data tab. All three now count by the sourcetype's inventory scope, and mapped means mapped to any CIM model. Sourcetypes missing from the inventory fall back to the categories of the models they map to; the Unmapped Data tab applies the same fallback.

Short Description:
See your Docker, Compose, Swarm, Podman and Amazon ECS hosts in Splunk: container and host logs and Docker events in an events index, host, container and process stats in the events index or a metrics index. Dashboards that lead to what needs fixing, and 61 alert templates each team scopes to its own clusters. One Collectord container per host.


Description:
Monitoring Docker brings the hosts that run your containers into Splunk: Docker hosts and Compose projects, Docker Swarm clusters, Podman hosts, and Amazon ECS container instances. Containers fail in ways their logs alone don't explain. A container restarts in a loop, is OOM killed, or fails its health check. A Swarm service runs fewer tasks than it should, and the reason is in the Swarm's services, tasks and nodes, which only a manager can read. The Docker data root fills up with images, writable layers and json-file logs. Some containers run their processes as root or hold Linux capabilities. The answers are spread over every host, in the logs, the cgroups, /proc and the Docker API. Monitoring Docker shows what Collectord forwards from each host, where it runs as one container. Collectord sends container and host logs, the Docker daemon's events, and the containers, images, volumes and Swarm objects it reads from the API to an events index. Host, container, process, network, filesystem and disk stats go to the same events index, to a Splunk metrics index, or to both while you compare. The containers of rootless Podman users are monitored too. The app opens on an Overview that says whether anything needs attention and where: hosts whose stats went silent, Collectord problems, and containers OOM killed, in a restart loop, unhealthy or exited with a non-zero code. From there it drills down to hosts, containers and processes, Compose projects, Swarm services and nodes, ECS services, privileged containers, the network, filesystems, disk I/O and CPU throttling. Every stats dashboard has a twin that reads the metrics index, and the Configuration page chooses which set the menu shows. Name each cluster, such as prod or staging, and the dashboards and alerts filter by it. Alerts come from an Alert Catalog of 61 templates, written for Splunk admins, the platform team and application teams. Each team picks the alerts it needs and creates them as its own saved searches, scoped to its own clusters. Container labels configure one container at a time: its index and Splunk output, field extraction, multi-line events, masking, log files from its volumes, and Prometheus endpoints. Three features, off by default, send fewer events: repeated lines as one counted event, storms of alike lines folded into a summary a minute, and a report of each stream's heaviest log patterns. Install the app on your search heads, create an HTTP Event Collector token, and start Collectord on each host with docker run, Docker Compose, a Swarm stack, Podman, or an Amazon ECS daemon service. A service fails and systemd restarts it in a loop, and nobody notices. A host slows down, and nobody can tell whether it is CPU, memory pressure, I/O or one runaway process. A filesystem fills up, the connection tracking table fills and the kernel drops new connections, or security updates wait for weeks on a host nobody remembers. The answers sit in each host's journal and /proc, one host at a time. Monitoring Linux shows what Collectord forwards from each host. Description:
ROVIX Universal API Add-on for Splunk lets you bring data from any REST/JSON API into Splunk by filling in forms. No code or custom scripts are needed. The problem it solves Security and IT teams need data from dozens of cloud services: identity providers, EDR tools, SaaS platforms, threat-intelligence feeds and internal APIs. Many of these have no Splunk add-on, or the add-on is outdated or limited. The usual workarounds are custom Python scripts or one-off modular inputs. Each one handles OAuth tokens, pagination and “what did I already collect?” differently, breaks when a token expires, and is hard to maintain or hand over. What the add-on does One place for every API. Define an account (credentials and authentication) once, then create as many inputs as you need. Each input has its own endpoint, interval, index and sourcetype. Handles authentication for you. Supports OAuth 2.0 (client credentials, authorization code with automatic refresh-token rotation, password grant), JWT bearer and private_key_jwt (including Google service accounts), session login, HMAC request signing, API key, bearer token, Basic and Digest, plus mTLS. Tokens are stored encrypted in Splunk, refreshed before they expire, and renewed automatically if the API rejects them. Collects everything, exactly once. Built-in pagination (offset, page, cursor, Link header, next URL) fetches every page. Checkpoints in the KV Store pick up where the last run stopped, and only move forward after a run completes successfully, so data isn’t skipped. Built to keep running. Retries with back-off on rate limits (HTTP 429) and server errors, honouring Retry-After. A monitoring dashboard and per-input logs make problems easy to see. Who it’s for: Splunk admins and SOC teams who need to onboard API-based data sources quickly and reliably on Splunk Enterprise or Splunk Cloud Platform, without writing and maintaining code. The application also includes an autonomous triage worker. When Auto Triage is enabled, the scripted input runs every 60 seconds by default, identifies eligible unprocessed Splunk ES notable events, sends the complete event context for AI analysis, and writes the resulting triage report back to the notable event. Role-based access is provided through dv_ai_user, dv_ai_admin, and dv_ai_action roles. item.title: Nikhil Chawla Add-on for Cisco Secure Firewall eStreamer (FMC) - v2.2.1 [Version Update]
item.description:
Platform: Splunk


Release Notes:
2.2.1 (includes 2.2.0, which was not released separately) New \- All eStreamer event types, chosen per input: connection, policy violation (correlation), VPN login/logoff and FireAMP over the binary connection; file, intrusion and intrusion packet events over a second (FQE) connection, with the same request as the Cisco Security Cloud app's eStreamer input. \- CEF output (Write CEF): chosen events can also be written as CEF lines to files, for a syslog agent to forward. \- Inputs page: Index in Splunk, Write CEF and one checkbox per event type. \- CIM event types and tags for policy violation (Alerts), VPN (Network Sessions, Authentication) and FireAMP (Malware). CIM mapping on the search heads needs the Cisco Security Cloud app. \- Status dashboard is now a classic (Simple XML) dashboard with no automatic refresh and an Event index field. It carries its own searches, so it also works pasted onto a search head without the add-on. \- Record type counts and an optional raw sample for troubleshooting (see README). Fixed \- Event file names are never used twice. Before, a writer that started more than one file a second could reuse a deleted file's name, and Splunk or a syslog agent could skip the new file. Upgrading \- Install over 2.1.x and restart. Inputs keep collecting connection events for Splunk only, as before, until other event types or Write CEF are chosen. The search macros fmc_estreamer_logs and fmc_estreamer_events are removed.


Short Description:
High-volume collector for Cisco Secure Firewall (FMC) connection events over eStreamer. Indexes them as cisco:sfw:estreamer with the Cisco Security Cloud app's field names, so its CIM mappings and dashboards work. Inputs, certificates and status are managed in Splunk Web. Independent project, not affiliated with Cisco.


Description:
Collects connection events from a Cisco Secure Firewall Management Center (FMC) over eStreamer and indexes them as sourcetype cisco:sfw:estreamer, with the field names the Cisco Security Cloud app uses for that sourcetype (InitiatorIP, ResponderIP, FirewallRule, AC_RuleAction, ...). That app's field aliases, CIM mappings and dashboards therefore work on these events, and existing searches keep working. Busy FMCs send thousands of connection events per second. This add-on is built for that volume: each input decodes in parallel processes, keeps events on disk until Splunk has read them, and resumes from a bookmark after a restart, so a restart does not skip events. - One input per FMC, several FMCs per heavy forwarder - Inputs page in Splunk Web: add, edit, enable, disable and restart inputs, and upload the eStreamer client certificate (the PKCS12 file from the FMC, or PEM). Certificates are stored encrypted in Splunk's credential store. - Status dashboard: throughput, minutes behind the FMC, connects and errors, indexed volume and index delay per FMC - Names from the FMC's metadata: rules, access control policy (FirewallPolicy), prefilter policy (PrefilterPolicy), tunnel/prefilter rule (TunnelRule), zones, interfaces, devices, applications, URL categories and countries - host is a name you choose for each FMC; the FMC's address is in every event as SourceHost - Disk buffer with a size cap: files are deleted once Splunk has read them; when the buffer is full, delete the oldest files or pause - Python standard library only, no third-party packages Connection events only. Intrusion, file/malware and packet events can come from the Cisco Security Cloud app. Independent project, not affiliated with or endorsed by Cisco.
